children.name: Thematic Coding
children.blurb: Thematic coding is the family of qualitative techniques for marking segments of text or talk with labels and then grouping those labels into broader themes.

children.name: Interview Transcription and Speaker Separation
children.blurb: Interview transcription and speaker separation covers the conversion of recorded interviews into written text and the labelling of who spoke when.

children.name: Finding Patterns in Lived Experience
children.blurb: Finding patterns in lived experience is a qualitative and mixed methods research activity.

children.name: Ethnographic Synthesis
children.blurb: Ethnographic synthesis is the interpretive combination of findings from multiple ethnographic studies or fieldwork accounts.

children.name: Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Data
children.blurb: Combining qualitative and quantitative data means bringing together non-numeric evidence such as interviews, field notes, documents, or open-ended survey responses with numeric measures, counts, or model outputs.

sections.body: Qualitative analysis and mixed methods in AI research is the work of turning interviews, field notes, open ended survey answers, and other unstructured material into findings that can be compared with numbers. Artificial intelligence is actually doing this now through automatic speech recognition for interview transcription, speaker separation to tell who said what, and natural language processing to suggest themes or codes. Researchers use clustering and topic models to find patterns in lived experience, and they use summarization tools to help synthesize ethnographic notes. Mixed methods work links those themes to quantitative data, such as survey scores or sensor readings, so that one kind of evidence can inform the other. The aim is not to replace the researcher but to speed up repetitive steps and to make large qualitative corpora more tractable. These tools sit inside a longer tradition of coding, memoing, and interpretation that predates AI.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Transcription for clear, single speaker audio is largely solved, but overlapping speech, strong accents, poor recordings, and specialized vocabulary still produce errors that require human correction. Thematic coding can be assisted by AI that proposes labels or groups similar passages, yet the meaning of a code depends on context, research question, and the coder's judgment, so agreement between human coders remains a central check. Pattern finding in lived experience can surface repeated patterns and recurring narratives, but it can also amplify false patterns, bias in the source data, or the assumptions built into a model. Ethnographic synthesis is harder to automate because thick description, silence, irony, and cultural nuance often resist summarization. Combining qualitative and quantitative data is conceptually powerful but practically difficult, since the two kinds of data have different scales, sampling logics, and standards of evidence. The honest limit is that AI can organize and suggest, but it cannot take responsibility for interpretation, consent, privacy, or the ethical use of participant data.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section fit together as a sequence and a set of choices. Thematic Coding covers how codes are built, applied, and checked, and it is the place to go for the core analytic step. Interview Transcription and Speaker Separation deals with the earlier problem of turning audio into text and marking who spoke, which feeds every later stage. Finding Patterns in Lived Experience looks at how AI can help detect recurring themes, outliers, and narrative structures across many accounts. Ethnographic Synthesis addresses the slower work of field notes, observation, and cultural context, where the goal is depth rather than counting. Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Data explains how to bring themes and numbers into one design, including integration and triangulation. The site library holds 135 research papers, and these pages link to original papers rather than to a search tool, so a reader can follow the evidence back to its source.
